title: The State in Capitalist, Socialist, Developed and Developing Societies

cards.h: The state is not the same everywhere
cards.b:
Every country has a state, but states differ widely. A Swedish welfare state, a Soviet party-state, a developmental Korean state and a fragile state in the Sahel all claim to be "the state", yet they do very different things.

This lesson compares the state across capitalist, socialist, developed and developing societies. It builds on your Paper I work on theories of the state (liberal, Marxist, pluralist, post-colonial and feminist) and applies them across cases.

Expect questions that ask you to compare, such as "Distinguish between the state in developed and developing societies" or "Has globalisation weakened the state?" A strong answer uses a few typologies, thinkers with books and years (Weber, Tilly, Mann, Alavi, Migdal, Evans), and a quick set of country examples.

Always finish with India, which sits between categories: a democratic, developmental and welfare-seeking state in a poor, diverse society.

Max Weber, in "Politics as a Vocation" (1919), defined the state as the human community that successfully claims the monopoly of the legitimate use of physical force within a given territory.

Four features most scholars list

  • Territory with borders.
  • Population.
  • Government: institutions that make and enforce rules.
  • Sovereignty: supreme authority inside, independence outside.

Keep three terms apart: the state is the permanent apparatus, the government is the team in office, and the nation is a community of identity.

How states formed. Charles Tilly, "War Made the State, and the State Made War" (1975) and Coercion, Capital, and European States (1990): European rulers fought wars, so they raised taxes and built bureaucracies. In much of the Global South, states came from colonial rule or a negotiated independence, with weaker links between state and society.

Michael Mann (1984) separated despotic power (rulers acting without consent) from infrastructural power (the ability to reach into society and implement policy).

cards.h: Mann's two kinds of state power
cards.b:
Mann's four types are a helpful map. Western liberal democracies sit in the bureaucratic box: limited by law but able to tax, register and serve citizens.

Many developing states have a gap. They look strong on paper (a big army, wide laws) but cannot enforce rules across the territory.

cards.h: Theories of the state in brief
cards.b:
• Liberal and pluralist. The state is a neutral umpire between groups (Dahl, Who Governs?, 1961).
  • Marxist. Marx and Engels: "The executive of the modern State is but a committee for managing the common affairs of the whole bourgeoisie." Instrumentalist view: Ralph Miliband, The State in Capitalist Society (1969), pointed to business links with state elites. Structuralist view: Nicos Poulantzas, Political Power and Social Classes (1968): the state has relative autonomy and serves capital's long-term needs. Gramsci: the state is hegemony protected by the armour of coercion.
  • Elite theory. Mosca, Pareto: an organised minority rules.
  • State-centred. Theda Skocpol, Bringing the State Back In (1985): the state has interests and capacities of its own.
  • Feminist. The state reflects patriarchal power (Catharine MacKinnon, Carole Pateman).
  • Post-colonial. Hamza Alavi and Partha Chatterjee: the colonial inheritance shapes the state.

These theories are covered in depth in Paper I. Here we use them as lenses for comparison.

Capitalist states protect property and contracts, support markets, and usually combine this with welfare and regulation. Over time, the pattern shifted.

  • Laissez-faire/liberal state (19th century): minimal state, "night-watchman" (Nozick's later phrase).
  • Keynesian welfare state (1945-70s): full employment, health, education and social insurance. Beveridge Report (1942) and the UK NHS (1948) are landmarks. The Nordic social-democratic model went furthest.
  • Neoliberal state (from the 1980s): Thatcher and Reagan. Privatisation, deregulation, lower taxes, cuts in welfare, an independent central bank. Government became a regulator and facilitator.
  • Post-2008 and post-2020 state. Bailouts, pandemic spending, industrial policy and strategic controls on technology and trade, in the US and EU. Tariffs and subsidies in 2025-26 show that even market economies use the state to steer the economy.

Varieties exist: the US state is fragmented and market-oriented; the German state is coordinated; the French is more centralised and interventionist (dirigisme).

Socialist states, in the Marxist-Leninist model, claim to represent the working class.

  • Lenin, The State and Revolution (1917): the state is a tool of class rule. After revolution, a dictatorship of the proletariat would suppress the old class and then "wither away".
  • In practice: a one-party state with a vanguard party, a command economy, public ownership, central planning, and heavy control of media and society. The USSR from the 1920s and Eastern Europe after 1945.
  • Critique from within. Milovan Djilas, The New Class (1957): a party bureaucracy became a ruling class. The Soviet nomenklatura system gave privileges to party loyalists.
  • Achievements: literacy, health, industrialisation, and gender equality in law. Failures: shortages, low innovation, repression and the stifling of dissent.
  • Collapse. 1989-91 ended the Soviet model in Europe.

Debates on its nature: Trotsky called the USSR a "degenerated workers' state"; others called it "state capitalism" or bureaucratic collectivism.

Surviving socialist-led states changed course.

  • China. Deng Xiaoping's reforms (from 1978) opened the economy: household farming, special economic zones, WTO entry (2001). The Communist Party retains political control, calling it "socialism with Chinese characteristics". The state owns large firms and banks, directs investment, and uses industrial plans (Made in China 2025). Rapid growth lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty.
  • Vietnam. Doi Moi (1986) brought market reforms under one-party rule.
  • Cuba and North Korea remain more closed.

Ian Bremmer, The End of the Free Market (2010), called such models state capitalism: the state acts as the main economic actor for political gain. Critics note that corruption, local debt and weak private rights are risks. Supporters point to speed and strategy.

Scholars debate whether there is a "Beijing Consensus" (Joshua Cooper Ramo, 2004), an alternative to the Washington Consensus.

• Overdeveloped state. Hamza Alavi, "The State in Post-Colonial Societies: Pakistan and Bangladesh" (1972): colonial rulers built a large civil-military apparatus before local classes were strong. After independence, the state is relatively autonomous and dominated by a bureaucratic-military oligarchy, which stands above competing local classes.
  • Soft state. Gunnar Myrdal, Asian Drama (1968): the state cannot enforce its own rules and policies.
  • Quasi-states. Robert Jackson, Quasi-States (1990): in Africa, states exist because of external recognition of sovereignty, without strong internal capacity.
  • Weak states and strong societies. Joel Migdal, Strong Societies and Weak States (1988): local strongmen and chiefs challenge the state's rules.
  • Neo-patrimonial state. Nicolas van de Walle and Michael Bratton (1997): public office is used for private gain, through patronage.
  • Failed and fragile states. Robert Rotberg, When States Fail (2004): Somalia, Afghanistan, and others. Today's lists include Sudan, South Sudan, Yemen and Haiti.

Developmental state

South Korea, Taiwan, Japan, Singapore. A competent bureaucracy, close but autonomous ties with business (Peter Evans's embedded autonomy), export discipline, land reform and education first. Chalmers Johnson (1982), Alice Amsden (1989), Robert Wade (1990).

Predatory state

Rulers extract wealth for themselves and their circle. Zaire under Mobutu is Evans's classic case (Embedded Autonomy, 1995).

Rentier state

The state lives on external income, such as oil, so it does not need to tax citizens. Hossein Mahdavy (1970); Michael Ross, "Does Oil Hinder Democracy?" (2001). Saudi Arabia, Venezuela, Nigeria.

Why they differ

Colonial legacy, natural resources, geopolitics (Cold War aid), social structure (land reform, ethnic divisions), and leadership. Dani Rodrik and others stress policy and institutions.

Do states matter less today? The debate:

  • Retreat. Susan Strange, The Retreat of the State (1996): markets, firms and global finance limit what governments can do. Kenichi Ohmae spoke of the "end of the nation state" (1995).
  • Adaptation. The state is changing form, not shrinking. Governments regulate global firms, sign trade deals and manage borders. Linda Weiss, The Myth of the Powerless State (1998).
  • Return of the state. After 2008 and the pandemic, then the tariffs, subsidies and sanctions of 2022-26, states play a bigger economic role. National security now shapes trade and technology policy.
  • New pressures. Digital platforms, AI, migration, climate, and non-state armed groups all test state capacity.

Conclusion for exams: the state is not withering away. It is changing: from provider to regulator and security manager, with big differences between strong and weak states.

cards.h: The Indian state in comparative perspective
cards.b:
• Type. A democratic, developmental, welfare-seeking state in a poor and diverse society. It combines liberal-democratic form with a developmental purpose.
  • Phases. Nehruvian state (Planning Commission, 1950; mixed economy; public-sector "commanding heights"). The 1991 reforms made the state more of a regulator (SEBI, TRAI, CCI). Since 2014 the Planning Commission has been replaced by NITI Aayog (2015) and the state has used digital delivery (Aadhaar, UPI, DBT).
  • Welfare. A rights-based turn: MGNREGA (2005), RTI (2005), RTE (2009), National Food Security Act (2013).
  • Analyses. Bardhan: held back by the rivalry of dominant proprietary classes. Rudolph and Rudolph: a "command" and a "demand" polity. Atul Kohli: a "democratic developmental" state with mixed results. Partha Chatterjee: The Politics of the Governed (2004), political society: the poor negotiate with the state outside formal civil society. Sudipta Kaviraj on the "dialectic" of the Indian state.
  • Capacity gaps. A strong centre and army, but uneven delivery in health, policing and courts. This is the soft-state critique.

"Compare the nature of the state in developed and developing societies."
"Has globalisation weakened the state? Examine with reference to developing countries."
"Explain the 'overdeveloped' state thesis of Hamza Alavi."
"Distinguish between a developmental state and a predatory state."

Structure: define the state (Weber), note Mann's two powers. Give brief theories of the state. Then compare four types in a table: capitalist (liberal, welfare, neoliberal), socialist (Soviet, Chinese), developed (strong infrastructural power, welfare), developing (Alavi, Migdal, Jackson, developmental versus predatory). Add the globalisation debate. Close with India.

A two-column table (developed versus developing) is efficient and scores well.

quiz.w: Tilly's study of European state formation.

o: The power of rulers to act without consent
The state's ability to implement decisions throughout society

quiz.q: Ralph Miliband's The State in Capitalist Society (1969) is an example of which Marxist view?
quiz.w: He emphasised the links between business and state elites.

quiz.q: Hamza Alavi's 1972 article argued that post-colonial states are:
o: Overdeveloped and dominated by a bureaucratic-military oligarchy
quiz.w: The colonial apparatus preceded local class formation.

quiz.q: Robert Jackson's Quasi-States (1990) argues that many African states:
o: Survive on external recognition of sovereignty

quiz.q: Joel Migdal's Strong Societies and Weak States (1988) suggests:
o: Societies resist and bypass state rules
quiz.w: Local strongmen and social organisations compete with the state.

quiz.q: Who coined the 'new class' critique of Communist rule in 1957?
quiz.w: The party bureaucracy became a ruling class.
